facts.fact: Opened on 9 May 2015 at Largo Isarco as the Fondazione's new permanent Milan venue.
facts.quote: On 9 May 2015, the Fondazione Prada unveiled its new permanent Milan venue, in Largo Isarco.

facts.fact: OMA, led by Rem Koolhaas, conceived the venue.
facts.quote: The new Milan venue of the Fondazione, conceived by architecture firm OMA—led by Rem Koolhaas—expands the repertoire of spatial typologies in which art can be exhibited and shared with the public.

facts.fact: It transforms a former distillery from the 1910s, adding three new structures to the existing buildings.
facts.quote: The complex, which is the result of the transformation of a former distillery dating back to the 1910s, is articulated by an architectural configuration which combines preexisting buildings with three new structures, named “Podium”, “Cinema” and “Torre”.

facts.fact: The "Haunted House" is a four-storey building clad in gold foil that displays the permanent collection.
facts.quote: The hallmark of the new venue is the so-called “Haunted House”, a 4-story building, clad in 24 carat gold foil, where pieces from the permanent collection of art of the Fondazione Prada are permanently on display.

facts.fact: The film director Wes Anderson recreated the mood of old Milan cafés in the bar.
facts.quote: The entrance building welcomes visitors to two new facilities, developed through special collaborations: a kids' area designed by a group of students from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture de Versailles, and a bar where director Wes Anderson has recreated the typical mood of old Milan cafés.

facts.fact: Sultan Bayezid I commissioned it to mark his victory at the Battle of Nicopolis; it was built 1396–1399.
facts.quote: It was commissioned by the Ottoman Sultan Bayezid I to commemorate his great victory at the Battle of Nicopolis and built between 1396 and 1399.

facts.fact: It is a major monument of early Ottoman architecture in the old city beside the historic markets.
facts.quote: The mosque is a major monument of early Ottoman architecture and one of the most important mosques in the city, located in the heart of the old city alongside its historic markets.

facts.fact: Ali Neccar designed and built it.
facts.quote: Ordered by Sultan Bayezid I, the mosque was designed and built by architect Ali Neccar in 1396–1399.

facts.fact: Twenty domes in four rows of five sit on twelve columns.
facts.quote: Its interior space is covered by twenty domes arranged in four rows of five that are supported by twelve columns.

facts.fact: Tradition says the twenty domes stand in place of twenty separate mosques the Sultan had promised.
facts.quote: A popular tradition holds that Sultan Bayezid I built a mosque of twenty domes instead of building twenty separate mosques which he had promised in return for winning the Battle of Nicopolis in 1396.

facts.fact: A fountain under a dome open to the sky (now glazed) lights the interior and served ablutions.
facts.quote: The dome over the şadırvan is open to the sky (though covered by glass today), creating a skylight which helps to illuminate the mosque's dark interior.

facts.fact: It has three entrances, the northern one the most monumental.
facts.quote: It has three entrances (to the north, west and east), of which the northern entrance is the most monumental.

facts.fact: An earthquake in 1855 collapsed the roof and closed the mosque for years.
facts.quote: Following a damaging earthquake in 1855 which caused the roof to collapse, the mosque was closed for a number of years.

facts.fact: It is a passenger terminal for the annual Hajj pilgrimage at Jeddah's King Abdulaziz International Airport.
facts.quote: The Hajj Terminal is a passenger terminal dedicated to the annual Haji pilgrimage at King Abdulaziz International Airport, the principal airport serving Jeddah and Mecca, Saudi Arabia.

facts.fact: SOM won the design contract in 1975.
facts.quote: International architecture and engineering firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill won the contract for designing the terminal in 1975.

facts.fact: The architects based the design on traditional Bedouin tents rather than a standard enclosed building.
facts.quote: Instead of constructing a standard, enclosed building for the airport which would not reflect the kingdom's culture, the architects based it off traditional Bedouin tents.

facts.fact: Fazlur Khan wanted the main space to be open and shaded rather than fully air-conditioned.
facts.quote: We felt that from a local and cultural viewpoint, the main terminal space should be an open, shaded space.

facts.fact: The roof uses a translucent fibre sheet developed by Owens-Corning.
facts.quote: A translucent material developed by Owens-Corning produced a thin fibre sheet for the roof.

facts.fact: A terminal with permanent tents was unheard of at the time.
facts.quote: At the time, a terminal permanently incorporating tents was unheard of.

facts.fact: Hochtief was general contractor.
facts.quote: West German engineering firm, Hochtief was entrusted as the general contractor for the project.

facts.fact: Construction began in 1979 and finished in 1982 (the article's infobox gives an inauguration date of 31 May 1981).
facts.quote: Construction began in 1979, and was completed within a three-year timeframe in 1982.

facts.fact: It is in Hijiyama Park, Hiroshima.
facts.quote: It is in Hijiyama Park in Hiroshima, Japan.

facts.fact: Kisho Kurokawa designed the building.
facts.quote: The building was designed by architect Kisho Kurokawa.

facts.fact: It was the first public contemporary art museum to open in Japan.
facts.quote: It was the first public contemporary art museum to open in Japan, and its exhibitions focus on post-1945, contemporary emerging artists and artworks that link contemporary art with Hiroshima.

facts.fact: The museum was founded in 1989.
facts.quote: The Hiroshima City Museum of Contemporary Art (広島市現代美術館, Hiroshima-shi Gendai Bijutsukan) is an art museum founded in 1989.

facts.fact: It opened in 1971 as a centre for the performing arts.
facts.quote: The Jerusalem Theatre (Hebrew: תיאטרון ירושלים, a.k.a. The Jerusalem Centre for the Performing Arts) is a centre for the performing arts in Jerusalem.

facts.fact: A 1958 municipal design competition was won by Michael Nadler, Shulamit Nadler and Shmuel Bixson.
facts.quote: Architects Michael Nadler, Shulamit Nadler and Shmuel Bixson won first prize.

facts.fact: The complex has four performance halls of different sizes.
facts.quote: The complex consists of the Sherover Theatre, which seats 950, the Henry Crown Symphony Hall (home of the Jerusalem Symphony Orchestra) with 750 seats, the Rebecca Crown Auditorium, with 450 seats, and the Little Theatre with 110 seats.

facts.fact: Exposed concrete is combined with Jerusalem stone.
facts.quote: The theatre combines sculptural elements of exposed concrete with traditional Jerusalem stone construction.

facts.fact: It stands in a large public square used for outdoor events.
facts.quote: It sits in a large public square that is used for outdoor concerts and other events.

facts.fact: The Crown wing was designed by the same firm as a continuation of the original.
facts.quote: The planning and design of the new wing was carried out by the same architectural firm, so that the new wing, named for Crown's parents, was a natural continuation of the original design.

facts.fact: Building was slow, from the 1964 cornerstone to the 1971 dedication.
facts.quote: The building was dedicated in October 1971.

facts.fact: It was listed for preservation in 2012.
facts.quote: In 2012, the Jerusalem Theatre complex, together with the nearby Presidential Residence and the Van Leer Institute, was officially listed for historical preservation by the Jerusalem Municipality, reflecting its architectural and cultural significance in the city’s modern built environment.

facts.fact: It is an Edwardian building completed in 1914.
facts.quote: Johannesburg City Hall is an Edwardian building constructed in 1914 by the Hawkey and McKinley construction company.

facts.fact: A 1909 competition was open only to South African resident architects and judged by Leonard Stokes.
facts.quote: Only South African resident architects were allowed to take part and entries were judged by Leonard Stokes, Vice-President of the Royal Institute of British Architects and a decision was made in March 1910.

facts.fact: A Cape Town firm won the competition; a different man, Mattheus Meischke, won the building contract.
facts.quote: A Cape Town architectural firm, Hawke and McKinlay, won the competition to design the new building but it took until 17 February 1912 before Mattheus Meischke was awarded the tender to construct the building which would cost £503,000.

facts.fact: The style is Edwardian Baroque with an Ionic portico and a neo-Renaissance tower.
facts.quote: The style is described as Edwardian Baroque with a portico of Ionic columns and tower with a half dome entrance described as neo-Renaissance.

facts.fact: It has two halves: municipal offices to the east, the Town Hall to the west.
facts.quote: The building is designed as two-halves, with the eastern side consisting of the municipal offices which faces Rissik Street and the western side containing the Town Hall facing Harrison Street.

facts.fact: In 1937 the tower was taken down, a floor added, and the tower rebuilt.
facts.quote: In 1937, the City Hall would undergo further construction when the tower was dismantled and an additional floor was added to the building and then the tower rebuilt.

facts.fact: It became a National Monument in 1979.
facts.quote: On 12 October 1979, City Hall was designated a National Monument.

facts.fact: The Gauteng Provincial Legislature moved in during 1995.
facts.quote: After the 1994 South African elections, the Gauteng Provincial Legislature moved from Pretoria to Johannesburg and on 21 October 1995 the City Hall would become its new home.

facts.fact: It is a pedestrian shopping street designed by Jo van den Broek and Jaap Bakema to rebuild Rotterdam after the 1940 bombing; it opened 9 October 1953.
facts.quote: It was designed by Jo van den Broek and Jaap Bakema as part of the rebuilding of the city after the German bombing of 1940, and opened on 9 October 1953.

facts.fact: It has been described as the first purpose-built pedestrian street in Europe.
facts.quote: It has been described as the first purpose-built pedestrian street in Europe.

facts.fact: Shops face a car-free promenade, are serviced from streets behind, and housing sits in separate blocks.
facts.quote: The design separated the functions that had shared the pre-war streets. Shops lined a car-free promenade and were supplied from service streets behind them, while housing went into separate apartment blocks.

facts.fact: A 1:100 model won over the sceptical shopkeepers.
facts.quote: The 66 shopkeepers taking part were sceptical at first, but a model at 1:100 scale won them over.

facts.fact: Lewis Mumford praised it in 1957.
facts.quote: The American critic Lewis Mumford praised it in The New Yorker in 1957.

facts.fact: It was cited as a model abroad, such as Stevenage town centre.
facts.quote: The street has also been cited as a model for pedestrian shopping areas abroad, such as the town centre of Stevenage.

facts.fact: The original section became a national monument in 2010.
facts.quote: The original section has been a rijksmonument (national monument) since 2010.

facts.fact: The name refers to ropewalks once in the area.
facts.quote: They also objected to the name, which refers to the ropewalks once located in the area, and would have preferred to call the street the Promenade.

facts.fact: It is a high-speed station in Reggio Emilia on the Milan–Bologna line.
facts.quote: The station is located on the Milan–Bologna high-speed railway and Reggio Emilia-Guastalla railway.

facts.fact: A regional line has linked it to central Reggio Emilia since December 2013.
facts.quote: Since 15 December 2013 the station has been connected to the regional line Reggio Emilia-Guastalla railway, offering a connection to the centre of Reggio Emilia.

facts.fact: Lev Rudnev designed it; it is the tallest of Moscow's Stalinist "Seven Sisters" (1947–1953).
facts.quote: It was designed by Lev Rudnev as the headquarters of Moscow State University,  and is the tallest among the "Seven Sisters" constructed in Moscow between 1947 and 1953 in the Stalinist architectural style.

facts.fact: It was the tallest building in Europe from 1953 to 1990.
facts.quote: It was the tallest building in Europe for 37 years, from 1953 to 1990,  before being surpassed by the Messeturm in Germany.

facts.fact: Lower lateral towers and dormitory wings enclose a cour d'honneur courtyard with the central tower.
facts.quote: Lateral towers are lower than the central one; two 18 and 9 storey dormitory wings define, with the central corpus of the complex, a cour d'honneur courtyard.

facts.fact: Boris Iofan lost the commission after placing his draft on the edge of Sparrow Hills, a landslide-prone site.
facts.quote: The leading architect Boris Iofan bid for the skyscraper project in 1947 but the job was assigned to Lev Rudnev, because Iofan made a mistake placing his draft skyscraper right on the edge of Sparrow Hills, a site concerned with a potential landslide hazard.

facts.fact: Rudnev set the building back from the cliff.
facts.quote: He set the building 800 meters away from the cliff.

facts.fact: The tower was inaugurated on 1 September 1953 and has a steel framework.
facts.quote: The main tower, which consumed over 40,000 tons of steel for its framework and 130,000 cubic metres of concrete, was inaugurated on September 1, 1953.

facts.fact: Sculptures decorate the building, including a student couple by Vera Mukhina.
facts.quote: Among the statues which decorate the building is a sculpture by Vera Mukhina representing a couple of students and a statue by N. Tomsky of Mikhail Lomonosov (1711–1765), the founder of Moscow University.

facts.fact: The skyline inspired buildings such as Warsaw's Palace of Culture and Science.
facts.quote: The University skyline inspired various buildings in the socialist countries, like the Palace of Culture and Science in Warsaw, and also the logo of 1980 Moscow Olympic Games.

facts.fact: It is Singapore's flagship national library, in twin 16-storey blocks linked by bridges on the upper floors.
facts.quote: A subsidiary of the National Library Board (NLB), it consists of twin 16-storey blocks, linked by bridges on the upper floors, with three underground basements

facts.fact: It replaced the old National Library at Stamford Road, which closed in March 2004.
facts.quote: The current building, a 16-storey, two-block development situated in the city's Civic District, replaces the old National Library at Stamford Road, which closed on 31 March 2004.

facts.fact: Ken Yeang's firm T.R. Hamzah & Yeang won the design contract after he split from the first design team.
facts.quote: Ken Yeang co-founded a Malaysian architectural firm T.R. Hamzah & Yeang   based in Kuala Lumpur and the new firm was awarded the design contract for the National Library by the Ministry of National Development.

facts.fact: It was officially opened on 12 November 2005.
facts.quote: The library moved to its new home on 22 July 2005, and the building was officially opened on 12 November that year by the then-President S. R. Nathan.

facts.fact: A reference library and a public library share the building.
facts.quote: It is the flagship building of the National Library Board, bringing together the core functions of the old library by incorporating a reference library, known as the Lee Kong Chian Reference Library (simplified Chinese: 李光前参考图书馆; traditional Chinese: 李光前參考圖書館; pinyin: Lǐguāngqián cānkǎo túshū guǎn), as well as a public library, the Central Public Library, under one roof.

facts.fact: A large bubble-like room called The Pod sits on the top level.
facts.quote: On the highest 16th level rooftop, there is a large closed area designed like a bubble called The Pod, used for functions and events.

facts.fact: Old bricks from the earlier library were reused.
facts.quote: A number of old bricks from the old National Library building has been incorporated into the present building.

facts.fact: The courthouse was first proposed in 1925 to replace seven small judicial offices.
facts.quote: The concept of constructing a new courthouse in Porta Vittoria to replace the seven small and outdated judicial offices then existing in Milan was initially proposed in 1925.

facts.fact: Marcello Piacentini, with Ernesto Rapisardi, designed it; it was finished in July 1940.
facts.quote: In collaboration with architect Ernesto Rapisardi, Piacentini designed and supervised the construction of the new courthouse, which was ultimated in July 1940.

facts.fact: One building holds three judicial institutions.
facts.quote: The building is an imposing structure situated on a centrally located site, conceived as a unified edifice housing three distinct judicial institutions: the Court of Appeal (Corte d'Appello), the Court (Tribunale), and the Magistrates Court (Pretura).

facts.fact: A tower stands at the southwest corner.
facts.quote: At the southwest corner stands a tower rising 61 meters high, originally intended to house the Archive.

facts.fact: It is mainly reinforced concrete with stone and marble decoration inside.
facts.quote: Constructed predominantly with reinforced concrete, the courthouse's interior features decorative elements crafted from precious stones and marble.

facts.fact: The exterior is austere while the interior is richly decorated.
facts.quote: While the exterior of the building presents a restrained and somewhat austere appearance, the interior is richly adorned with artistic embellishments, including bas-reliefs, mosaics, frescoes, and sculptures.

facts.fact: Artists including Mario Sironi and Fausto Melotti made the decoration.
facts.quote: These decorative works were realized by various prominent artists, notably Mario Sironi, Fausto Melotti, Carlo Carrà, Romano Romanelli, Achille Funi, and Arturo Dazzi.

facts.fact: The 2,400-seat hall by Jean Nouvel is the core of a complex in Parc de la Villette; it opened in January 2015.
facts.quote: At the core of this set of spaces is the symphonic concert hall of 2,400 seats designed by Jean Nouvel and opened in January 2015.

facts.fact: Its construction was postponed about twenty years to finish the Cité de la Musique first.
facts.quote: Its construction had been postponed for about twenty years to complete the current musical institution la Cité de la Musique designed by Christian de Portzamparc and opened in 1995.

facts.fact: Nouvel won the design competition in April 2007.
facts.quote: The renowned French architect Jean Nouvel won the design competition for the building in April 2007.

facts.fact: Nouvel worked with acousticians and a scenographer.
facts.quote: He brought in Brigitte Métra as his partner, along with Marshall Day Acoustics (room acoustics design) and Nagata Acoustics (peer-review and scale model study) and dUCKS Scéno (scenography).

facts.fact: Floating balconies keep the farthest listener close to the conductor.
facts.quote: The acoustic and architectural characteristics of the main concert hall have been described as "retaining a real sense of intimacy" which is "achieved by various floating balconies that enable even the farthest spectator to be only 36 yards away from the conductor."

facts.fact: A rooftop Belvedere has a path winding down to the park.
facts.quote: From the Belvedere on the roof where the Eiffel Tower can be seen a path snakes downward to the park.

facts.fact: Nouvel missed the opening concert amid a dispute over cost and completion date.
facts.quote: The opening concert was attended by French President François Hollande, the President of France  but not by Jean Nouvel, because of an ongoing dispute about the final costs and date of the building's completion.

facts.fact: It is a public art museum on the South Saskatchewan River in Saskatoon.
facts.quote: The art museum is situated along the west bank of the South Saskatchewan River, at the River Landing development in Saskatoon's Central Business District.

facts.fact: Bruce Kuwabara of KPMB Architects designed it with Architecture49.
facts.quote: The museum's 11,582 square metres (124,670 sq ft) building was designed by Bruce Kuwabara of KPMB Architects in association with Architecture49.

facts.fact: Construction ran from June 2013 and it opened in October 2017.
facts.quote: Construction for the art museum took place from June 2013 to 2017, and was opened to the public in October 2017.

facts.fact: The design draws on Prairie style and the region's barns, sheds and silos.
facts.quote: The building's design is influenced by Frank Lloyd Wright's Prairie style. The design of the building's exterior was based on region's open prairie landscape, and the barns, field sheds, and silos that occupy that space.

facts.fact: Cantilevered stacks extend toward the river and the skin is glass and copper mesh.
facts.quote: The exterior features cantilevered stacks that extend towards the South Saskatchewan River; and its glass and copper mesh exterior.

facts.fact: The steel mesh is a solar shading device.
facts.quote: The exterior steel mesh is a solar shading device and provides a shadowing effect on the building as the sun arcs through the sky.

facts.fact: The atrium rises to the fourth level with glass walls overlooking the river.
facts.quote: The "openness" of the prairie landscape were also reflected in the interior design of the building, with the ceiling of the main atrium extending to the fourth level of the building, and its walls being made of glass and overlooking the South Saskatchewan River.

facts.fact: It is the current meeting place of Thailand's National Assembly, on the Chao Phraya River in Bangkok.
facts.quote: It is located in Bangkok on the east bank of the Chao Phraya River in Kiakkai neighbourhood of the Dusit District.

facts.fact: A team led by Theerapol Niyom won the design competition.
facts.quote: Sappaya-Sapasathan was designed by a team led by Theerapol Niyom, who was the winner in the building's design competition.

facts.fact: Its main features include a central Thai pagoda, two chambers named for the Sun and the Moon, and teak.
facts.quote: Its main features are a Thai pagoda in the center of the building, Surya Hall (Hall of the Sun) for House of Representative, Chandra Hall (Hall of the Moon) for Senate of Thailand, and the use of 5,018 teak trees as they represent the "DNA of Thailand".

facts.fact: The design was inspired by a Thai Buddhist tale and made to look like a temple.
facts.quote: The building's design was inspired by a classic Thai Buddhist tale, Trai Bhum Phra Ruang, and was made to look like a temple as a reminder to officials of "Thainess" and morality, making it truly a Sappaya Sapasathan, "peaceful parliament".

facts.fact: It also houses museums, a convention center and offices.
facts.quote: It also houses museums, a convention center, a seminar room, a banquet hall, and offices.

facts.fact: The design has been criticised as "religious architecture".
facts.quote: The design has been criticised for being "religious architecture", embracing "elements of Buddhist and Hindu cosmology".

facts.fact: It opened officially on 1 May 2021 after delays and a budget rise.
facts.quote: The building was officially opened on 1 May 2021 after significant delays.

facts.fact: Philip Johnson designed it; it is made of Italian travertine with a grand hall and a distinctive central staircase.
facts.quote: The building, designed by architect Philip Johnson and funded by siblings Mary Frances and Adams Bromley Sheldon, is made of Italian travertine, featuring a grand hall and distinctive central staircase.

facts.fact: It was the dedicated home for the university's art collection from 1963.
facts.quote: The museum was established in 1963 when the university's art collection was moved to dedicated building at 451 North 12th Street.

facts.fact: The great hall has a suspended grand staircase.
facts.quote: The building, constructed of Italian travertine, includes an ornate great hall and a suspended grand staircase.

facts.fact: Isamu Noguchi made a work for the grand hall for the opening.
facts.quote: Japanese-American sculptor Isamu Noguchi was invited to create and install a work in the grand hall, which he titled "Song of the Bird," as part of the building's opening ceremonies.

facts.fact: Johnson called it the best building he ever designed.
facts.quote: Architect Philip Johnson proclaimed the Sheldon the best building he ever designed

facts.fact: It was designed to avoid "museum fatigue".
facts.quote: The building was designed to avoid what Johnson called "museum fatigue," a state of physical or mental exhaustion common among museum patrons.

facts.fact: The Sheldon siblings funded the project.
facts.quote: The siblings funded the entire project, combining to give over $1.5 million.

facts.fact: It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2013.
facts.quote: It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2013.

facts.fact: It is a mausoleum in Mashhad, designed by Hooshang Seyhoun and completed in 1963.
facts.quote: Designed by Hooshang Seyhoun and completed in 1963, the structure contains the grave of Nader Shah.

facts.fact: It was added to Iran's National Heritage List in 1975.
facts.quote: The structure was added to the Iran National Heritage List on 9 December 1975, administered by the Cultural Heritage, Handicrafts and Tourism Organization of Iran.

facts.fact: Nader Shah's body went uncommemorated until the 1960s.
facts.quote: Nader Shah's body remained un-commemorated until the 1960s when a concrete monument was constructed for him in the vicinity of a heavily polluted traffic intersection in Mashhad.

facts.fact: Nader Shah had ordered Mughal architects to build the Sun Palace as a jewel store and possible mausoleum.
facts.quote: Nader ordered the Mughal architects he had brought with himself to build the Sun Palace to store the jewels and possibly act as a mausoleum for him.

facts.fact: Gordon Bunshaft of SOM designed it.
facts.quote: It was designed by the prominent New York architect Gordon Bunshaft of the architectural firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill LLP.

facts.fact: It was completed in 1965 as the company headquarters and still serves that purpose.
facts.quote: It was completed in 1965 for the insurance company's headquarters and it continues to serve that purpose.

facts.fact: The east and west walls have no windows; north and south windows admit daylight and keep out radiant heat.
facts.quote: The Modernist building has no windows on its east and west elevations. The windows on the north and south elevations allow in daylight and keep out radiant heat.

facts.fact: It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2015.
facts.quote: It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2015.

facts.fact: It is the oldest performing-arts school in modern Greece, founded in 1871.
facts.quote: The Athens Conservatoire (Greek: Ωδείον Αθηνών, romanized: Odeíon Athinón) is the oldest educational institution for the performing arts in modern Greece.

facts.fact: Ioannis Despotopoulos, who studied under Walter Gropius, designed the building.
facts.quote: Designed by the Greek architect Ioannis Despotopoulos (also known as Jan Despo), the only Greek to have studied under Bauhaus school founder Walter Gropius, the Conservatoire is the only completed part of an ambitious large-scale cultural complex commissioned in 1959 by the then government for Athens, for which he earned the top architectural prize of its time.

facts.fact: It is described as an example of Bauhaus and the modern movement in Greece.
facts.quote: It is an exceptional example of the Bauhaus school and the modern movement in Greece.

facts.fact: Building began in 1969 and stopped in 1976 for lack of funds.
facts.quote: The construction begun in 1969 and stopped in 1976, due to a lack of funding, leaving the building unfinished.

facts.fact: The state paid for completion in 1980 in exchange for the old headquarters.
facts.quote: In 1980, the Greek state undertook the cost of completing the work in exchange for ownership of the conservatory's old headquarters on Pireos Street.

facts.fact: Despotopoulos's wider plan included an opera house and a National Gallery extension, but only the Conservatoire was built.
facts.quote: According to Despotopoulos' archives on file at the Modern Greek Architecture section of the Benaki Museum, in addition to the Athens Conservatoire, his plan foresaw the construction of an 1,800-seat opera house, a circular theatre stage, an extension to the National Gallery, a new Byzantine Museum, a Byzantine-style church, a hotel, a hall for classical dance performances and the state orchestra, a playhouse for experimental theater, underground garages and more.

facts.fact: Underground floors housed the National Museum of Contemporary Art from 2008 to 2015.
facts.quote: A large part of the underground floors of the building was used to host the National Museum of Contemporary Art, Athens (EMST), between September 2008 and May 2015.

facts.fact: It is the largest public museum in Bahrain, in Manama, and opened 15 December 1988.
facts.quote: Opened on 15 December 1988 by the Emir of Bahrain Isa bin Salman Al Khalifa, the $30 million museum complex covers 27,800 sq meters and is the country's most popular tourist attraction.

facts.fact: It is considered the region's first modern museum.
facts.quote: It is widely considered to be the region's first modern museum.

facts.fact: Danish architects Krohn & Hartvig Rasmussen designed it.
facts.quote: The modern museum was designed by Danish architects Krohn & Hartvig Rasmussen and officially opened in December 1988.

facts.fact: It stands on an artificial peninsula overlooking Muharraq.
facts.quote: It was constructed on an artificial peninsula overlooking the neighbouring island of Muharraq.

facts.fact: It has two buildings and six permanent exhibitions.
facts.quote: The museum is made of two buildings spanning a floor space of 20,000 square meters.

facts.fact: A UNESCO agreement in 1967 helped pave the way for a national museum.
facts.quote: In 1967, a cultural agreement was signed between UNESCO and the Bahraini government which helped pave the way for the construction of a national museum.

facts.fact: Konstantin Melnikov designed it in 1926 with Vladimir Shukhov as structural engineer; completed 1927.
facts.quote: Bakhmetevsky Bus Garage was a public bus garage in Moscow, designed in 1926 by Konstantin Melnikov (floorplan concept and architectural design) and Vladimir Shukhov (structural engineering).

facts.fact: It applied avant-garde methods to an industrial building.
facts.quote: The building, completed in 1927, was an example of applying avant-garde architectural methods to an industrial facility.

facts.fact: Melnikov sold the city on a free-flow garage layout.
facts.quote: He approached city transportation board and sold his idea for a free-flow garage.

facts.fact: It is red-brick industrial in look; circular attic windows are its only avant-garde feature.
facts.quote: Bakhmetevsky Garage, sometimes associated with constructivist architecture, was in fact styled in an indefinite red-brick industrial livery; circular windows in the attic are the only avant-garde features (and even these were destroyed decades ago).

facts.fact: A parallelogram-shaped garage sits on a rectangular lot, with workshops and offices filling the gaps.
facts.quote: Melnikov also designed workshops and office buildings on the same lot, filling the irregular voids made by placing a parallelogram-shaped garage on a larger, rectangular lot.

facts.fact: It was restored in 2007–2008 and reopened as a modern art gallery.
facts.quote: Neglected for decades and nearly condemned to demolition, it was restored in 2007–2008 and reopened in September 2008 as a gallery of modern art.

facts.fact: It is a preserved coal-fired power station on the south bank of the Thames.
facts.quote: Battersea Power Station is a preserved coal-fired power station located on the south bank of the River Thames in Nine Elms in the London Borough of Wandsworth.

facts.fact: J. Theo Halliday and Giles Gilbert Scott were the architects.
facts.quote: The architects were J. Theo Halliday and Giles Gilbert Scott.

facts.fact: It is one of the world's largest brick buildings with Art Deco interior fittings.
facts.quote: The station is one of the world's largest brick buildings and notable for its original, Art Deco interior fittings and decor.

facts.fact: It was built in two stages with a near-identical design, giving four chimneys.
facts.quote: Battersea B was built to a design nearly identical to that of Battersea A, creating the iconic four-chimney structure.

facts.fact: A was built 1929–1935 and B 1937–1941, completed in 1955.
facts.quote: Battersea A Power Station was built between 1929 and 1935 and Battersea B Power Station, to its east, between 1937 and 1941, when construction was paused owing to the worsening effects of the Second World War.

facts.fact: It was Grade II listed in 1980 and upgraded to Grade II* in 2007.
facts.quote: In 1980 the whole structure was given Grade II listed status; Battersea B shut three years later. In 2007 its listed status was upgraded to Grade II*.

facts.fact: It opened to the public after redevelopment in October 2022.
facts.quote: The main Power Station building was opened to the public in October 2022.

facts.fact: It appears on Pink Floyd's 1977 album Animals.
facts.quote: The station is also notable for its appearance on the cover of rock band Pink Floyd's 1977 studio album Animals.

facts.fact: It is a museum of Beirut's history, especially the Lebanese Civil War, in the restored Barakat building.
facts.quote: Beit Beirut (Arabic: بيت بيروت; literally "the house of Beirut") is a museum and urban cultural center dedicated to portraying the history of Beirut, with a particular focus on the Lebanese Civil War.

facts.fact: Youssef Aftimus designed the house in 1924 for Nicholas and Victoria Barakat.
facts.quote: Lebanese architect Youssef Aftimus, who designed Beirut's city hall, created and built the house in 1924.

facts.fact: Fouad Kozah added two storeys in 1932.
facts.quote: Architect Fouad Kozah added two more stories in 1932, giving the building its current form.

facts.fact: Its position on the demarcation line made it a sniper post in the civil war.
facts.quote: Its airy architecture and location on the demarcation line controlling the Sodeco crossroad made it strategically important.

facts.fact: Heritage activists saved it from a 1997 demolition decision.
facts.quote: It was saved by Lebanese heritage activists, particularly architect Mona Hallak who first investigated the house in 1994 during one of her visits with the "Association pour la Protection des Sites et Anciennes Demeures au Liban" (APSAD), an independent organisation for the protection of historic monuments and buildings.

facts.fact: Youssef Haidar led the restoration, which finished in 2016.
facts.quote: In 2009, Lebanese architect Youssef Haider was commissioned by the Beirut municipality to lead the building's restoration works.

facts.fact: A modern annex was planned on the empty lot around it.
facts.quote: The decree also provisions the construction of a modern annex to the building on the empty lot around it, which will house offices of the municipality's urban planning department as well as an underground parking lot.

facts.fact: It is the largest building with cultural facilities in Portugal.
facts.quote: It is the largest building with cultural facilities in Portugal, with over 140,000 m  (1,500,000 sq ft) of usable space.

facts.fact: It was built to host Portugal's 1992 EU Council presidency, then serve as a permanent venue.
facts.quote: The centre was initially built to accommodate the programme of Portugal's Presidency of the European Council in 1992, but with the long-term goal of providing permanent venues for conferences, exhibitions and performance arts (such as opera, ballet and concerts), in addition to meeting halls, shops and cafés.

facts.fact: Vittorio Gregotti and Atelier Risco, led by Manuel Salgado, won an international competition.
facts.quote: The final proposal, submitted by the architectural consortium of Vittorio Gregotti (Italy) and Atelier Risco at the time led by Manuel Salgado (Portugal), was designed to include five modules: a Conference Centre, a Performing Arts Centre, an Exhibition Centre, a Hotel and complementary equipment zone, but the Conference Centre, the Performing Arts Centre and the Exhibition Centre were initially built.

facts.fact: It sits beside the Jerónimos Monastery among historic buildings.
facts.quote: Apart from fronting the Praça do Império (Imperial Square), it juxtapositions the Jerónimos Monastery, and is surrounded by many historical buildings, such as the Palace and Tower of Belém, National Museum of Archaeology, Planetarium, and Monument to the Discoveries.

facts.fact: Waterfront buildings were demolished from 1989, and modules 1–3 were ready by January 1992.
facts.quote: By January 1992, modules 1, 2 and 3 were completed and ready to accommodate the institutions, administration, communication centre and security of the European Union Presidency.

facts.fact: A 57-entry competition was narrowed to six proposals.
facts.quote: An international architectural competition was held and six proposals were invited to submit a preliminary project, out of the 57 submissions.

facts.fact: It holds the world's largest collection of work by the Die Brücke expressionists.
facts.quote: The Brücke Museum in Berlin houses the world's largest collection of works by members of the group Die Brücke ("The Bridge"), an early 20th-century German expressionist movement.

facts.fact: It opened in 1967.
facts.quote: Opened in 1967, it features around 400 paintings and sculptures and several thousand drawings, watercolours and prints by members of Die Brücke, the movement founded in 1905 in Dresden.

facts.fact: It stands in a natural setting in Dahlem.
facts.quote: The museum is located in an idyllic natural setting in Dahlem, not far from the former studio of the sculptor Arno Breker.

facts.fact: It is a six-storey office building in Seattle designed to be the greenest commercial building in the world.
facts.quote: The Bullitt Center was designed to be the greenest commercial building in the world, and was certified as a "Living Building" by the International Living Future Institute in April 2015.

facts.fact: It was designed for a 250-year lifespan.
facts.quote: The Bullitt Center was designed to have a 250-year lifespan.

facts.fact: Roof solar panels let it produce more energy than it used in 2016.
facts.quote: In 2016, the Bullitt Center produced nearly 30 percent more energy than it needed for all uses, from the solar panels on its roof.

facts.fact: A rooftop array of 575 panels and conservation measures cut energy use to about 15% of a typical office.
facts.quote: Energy is generated by a large solar panel array (composed of 575 panels) on the roof of the building, along with energy conservation measures that cut the building's energy consumption to approximately 15% of a typical office building of similar size.

facts.fact: It has an on-site rainwater-to-potable water system and composting toilets.
facts.quote: Other features of the building include an onsite rainwater-to-potable water system, which will filter collected rainwater for all purposes once it is approved by regulators. There is also an onsite composting toilet system, the world's only 6-story system of its kind.

facts.fact: Geothermal wells help heat the building.
facts.quote: Additional features include 26 geothermal wells that extend 400 feet (120 m) into the ground, where the temperature is a constant 55 °F (13 °C).

facts.fact: Suppliers agreed to leave out toxic chemicals from materials.
facts.quote: The builders have negotiated with building material suppliers to ensure their products did not contain any of over 360 toxic chemicals;

facts.fact: The Bullitt Foundation built it.
facts.quote: It was built by the Bullitt Foundation, a non-profit group based in Seattle that focuses on urban ecology.

facts.fact: It is a Glasgow museum for Sir William Burrell's collection; it opened in 1983 and reopened in 2022 after refurbishment.
facts.quote: The museum opened in 1983 and reopened on 29 March 2022 following a major refurbishment.

facts.fact: A 1970 architectural competition was won by Barry Gasson with John Meunier and Brit Andresen.
facts.quote: The closing date for the competition for the museum building in 1971 was delayed by a postal strike, allowing time for the eventual winning architect Barry Gasson to complete his entry, designed in collaboration with John Meunier and Brit Andresen, all tutors at Cambridge University's School of Architecture.

facts.fact: Burrell's gift required the museum to be a separate building in a rural setting away from the city.
facts.quote: A memorandum of agreement between William and Constance and the Corporation of Glasgow was signed in April 1944. Burrell had clear intentions regarding the collection's location, contents and display, and the agreement stated that the collection was to be housed by Glasgow Corporation "in a suitable distinct and separated building" that was to be "within four miles [six kilometres] of Killearn, Stirlingshire, and not less than sixteen miles [26 kilometres] from Glasgow Royal exchange."

facts.fact: The orientation brings in natural light while protecting fragile pieces; the design was influenced by Scandinavian design.
facts.quote: The architects used the orientation of the building to bring in as much natural light as possible, while still protecting the vulnerable parts of the collection.

facts.fact: Objects such as Romanesque doorways are built into the structure.
facts.quote: The building is L-shaped in plan and is tailored to house and display the collection, with larger pieces such as Romanesque doorways built into the structure, at the same time giving views out into the park over formal grassed areas to the south and into adjacent woodland to the north.

facts.fact: The entrance uses a 16th-century stone archway set in a red sandstone gable, leading to a glazed central courtyard.
facts.quote: The entrance, through a 16th-century stone archway built into a modern red sandstone gable, leads to a shop and other facilities, then on to a central courtyard under a glazed roof, adjacent to the reconstructions of three rooms from the Burrells' home, Hutton Castle near Berwick-on-Tweed:  the wood-panelled drawing room, hall, and dining room complete with their furnishings.

facts.fact: Architects ranked it Scotland's second greatest post-war building in 2005.
facts.quote: It was named as Scotland's second greatest post-war building (after Gillespie, Kidd & Coia's St Peter's Seminary, now derelict) in a poll of architects by Prospect magazine in 2005.

facts.fact: It is a free-standing concrete tower on Gezira Island, tallest structure in Egypt until 1998.
facts.quote: At 187 m (614 ft), it was the tallest structure in Egypt for 37 years until 1998, when it was surpassed by the Suez Canal overhead powerline crossing.

facts.fact: Naoum Shebib designed it, built 1956 to 1961, inspired by ancient Egyptian architecture.
facts.quote: Built from 1956 to 1961, the tower was designed by the Egyptian architect Naoum Shebib, inspired by the ancient Egyptian architecture.

facts.fact: Its lattice-work design is intended to evoke a pharaonic lotus plant.
facts.quote: Its partially open lattice-work design is intended to evoke a pharaonic lotus plant, an iconic symbol of Ancient Egypt.

facts.fact: A circular observation deck and revolving restaurant crown it.
facts.quote: The tower is crowned by a circular observation deck and a revolving restaurant  that rotates around its axis occasionally  with a view over greater Cairo.

facts.fact: Its funding is said (in documents by Major General Adel Shaheen) to come from US money Nasser redirected.
facts.quote: According to documents published by Major General Adel Shaheen, the funds for the construction of the tower were originated from the Government of the United States through the CIA, represented by Kermit Roosevelt, which had provided around $US1-3 million to Gamal Abdel Nasser as a personal gift to him with the intent of stopping his support for Algerian Revolution and other African independence movements.

facts.fact: It was restored from 2006 to 2009.
facts.quote: Between 2006 and 2009, the tower underwent an £E15 million restoration by the Egyptian Arab Contractors Company.

facts.fact: It is sometimes considered Egypt's second most famous landmark.
facts.quote: One of Cairo's well-known modern monuments, sometimes considered Egypt's second most famous landmark after the Pyramids of Giza, it stands in the Gezira  district on Gezira Island in the River Nile, close to downtown Cairo.

facts.fact: It was built as the headquarters of the third UNCTAD conference held in Santiago in 1972.
facts.quote: The complex was originally built to serve as the headquarters for the third UNCTAD conference,  which was held in Santiago in 1972, and consisted of a convention centre and an adjoining 22-story building.

facts.fact: It was finished in 275 days with several thousand volunteers.
facts.quote: The building was finished in only 275 days in a significant effort supported by several thousand volunteers.

facts.fact: It later served as a military headquarters and as a Ministry of Defence building.
facts.quote: During the 1980's and 1990's, the building was known as the Edificio Diego Portales (Diego Portales building) and used as a military headquarters, where it was guarded and not open to the public.

facts.fact: A fire in 2006 led the government to return it to cultural use.
facts.quote: In early 2006, a fire destroyed parts of the building, which led the government of Michelle Bachelet to rethink the original sense of the building and return it to a cultural centre.

facts.fact: It was inaugurated as a cultural centre in September 2010.
facts.quote: The Centro Cultural Gabriela Mistral was inaugurated in September 2010  and is named after Gabriela Mistral.

facts.fact: It was the largest national pavilion at the Shanghai Expo and was later converted to the China Art Museum.
facts.quote: After the end of the Expo 2010, the building was converted to a museum. On October 1, 2012, it was reopened as the China Art Museum, the largest art museum in Asia.

facts.fact: The design was chosen from 344 proposals; He Jingtang was chief architect.
facts.quote: The chosen design was selected from a range of 344 design proposals put forward by architects from all over the world.

facts.fact: It is called the "Oriental Crown", and is the tallest structure at the Expo.
facts.quote: The 63-metre high pavilion, the tallest structure at the Expo, is dubbed "The Oriental Crown" because of its resemblance to an ancient Chinese crown.

facts.fact: The form draws on the dougong bracket and the ding vessel.
facts.quote: The architectonic feature of the building was inspired by the Chinese roof bracket known as the dougong  as well as the Chinese ding vessel.

facts.fact: Four giant columns resemble ding legs and the inverted pyramid body resembles the bowl.
facts.quote: The China pavilion's four giant columns resemble the legs of a ding vessel while the inverted pyramid body resembles the bowl of a vessel.

facts.fact: The roof is a grid pattern reminiscent of Jiugongge, the basis of ancient Chinese urban planning.
facts.quote: The rooftop of the building is in the shape of a grid-like pattern reminiscent of Jiugongge when view from the air.

facts.fact: Construction ran from December 2007 to November 2009.
facts.quote: The construction of the China pavilion began on 18 December 2007 and was completed in November 2009.

facts.fact: It was built in 1987 for the Universiade held in Zagreb that year.
facts.quote: The tower was built in 1987 because of the Universiade that was held in Zagreb that year.

facts.fact: Marijan Hržić was the architect.
facts.quote: The architect responsible for its design is Marijan Hržić.

facts.fact: It is a cylinder that narrows in four stages up to a radio mast.
facts.quote: The skyscraper is a cylinder, 25 m (82 ft) in diameter, which reduces its diameter in four stages, and ends up with a radio mast.

facts.fact: The facade combines dark steel, reflective glass and black granite.
facts.quote: The facade is derived in dark steel, totally reflective glass, and black granite.

facts.fact: 26 reinforced-concrete pylons hold the rim and make it earthquake resistant.
facts.quote: The rim of the tower is held by the 26 reinforced concrete pylons, which make it resistant to a 7° Richter scale earthquake, and the impact of a smaller airplane.

facts.fact: It belongs to a complex with a basketball hall.
facts.quote: The tower is a part of the complex that comprises lower business objects, a 5,400-seat basketball hall, and an art installation.

facts.fact: A renovation began in 2023 after a 2022 sale.
facts.quote: Cibona Tower was bought by the company Agram in 2022.  Since 2023 the business tower is being renovated.

facts.fact: Its acoustics rank it among the finest concert halls in the world.
facts.quote: Its superb acoustics place it among the finest concert halls in the world, along with New York's Carnegie Hall, Boston's Symphony Hall   and the Musikverein in Vienna.

facts.fact: Adolf Leonard van Gendt designed it, inspired by Leipzig's Gewandhaus.
facts.quote: The architect of the building was Adolf Leonard van Gendt [nl],  who was inspired by the Gewandhaus in Leipzig, built two years earlier (and destroyed in 1943).

facts.fact: It stands on 2,186 wooden piles.
facts.quote: A total of 2,186 wooden piles, 12 to 13 metres (40 to 43 ft) long, were emplaced in the soil.

facts.fact: It opened on 11 April 1888 after construction began in 1883.
facts.quote: The hall opened on 11 April 1888 with an inaugural concert, in which an orchestra of 120 musicians and a chorus of 500 singers participated, performing works of Wagner, Handel, Bach, and Beethoven.

facts.fact: It was built on a pasture then outside the city.
facts.quote: Construction began in 1883 in a pasture that was then outside the city,   in Nieuwer-Amstel, a municipality that in 1964 became Amstelveen.

facts.fact: It received the "Koninklijk" title in 2013.
facts.quote: In celebration of the building's 125th anniversary, Queen Beatrix bestowed the royal title "Koninklijk" upon the building on 11 April 2013, as she had on the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra upon its 100th in 1988.

facts.fact: It hosts some 900 events a year.
facts.quote: Today, some 900 concerts and other events per year take place in the Concertgebouw, for a public of over 700,000, making it one of the most-visited concert halls in the world.

facts.fact: Hack Kampmann and Aage Rafn designed it in 1918 in Neoclassical (Nordic Classicism) style; it was completed in 1924.
facts.quote: Designed by Hack Kampmann and Aage Rafn in 1918 in the Neoclassical style, often referred to as Nordic Classicism, it was completed in 1924.

facts.fact: Kampmann died in 1920, and Rafn exerted considerable influence on the design.
facts.quote: Hack Kampmann, who died in June 1920, did not live to see the completion of his building in early 1924.

facts.fact: It is said to be the last example of Neoclassical architecture in Northern Europe.
facts.quote: The building is said to be the last example of Neoclassical architecture in Northern Europe.

facts.fact: It is austere outside, with colourful interiors.
facts.quote: The outside of the building is intentionally austere, intensifying the attraction of the colourful, well-formed features inside, including dark terrazzo flooring and oversized door and window frames so meticulously crafted.

facts.fact: A round courtyard is ringed by 44 Doric columns.
facts.quote: The round courtyard, 45 m (148 ft) in width, is surrounded by a colonnade consisting of 44 Doric columns.

facts.fact: The foundations are 3,816 reinforced concrete piles.
facts.quote: Work on the foundations began in August of that year with 3,816 reinforced concrete piles.

facts.fact: Rafn took inspiration for the facade from London's dockland warehouses.
facts.quote: Rafn was inspired by the warehouses of London's dockland in designing the building's facade.

facts.fact: It is a housing building on the coast at Buceo, Montevideo.
facts.quote: The Panamericano Building is a housing construction located in the area Buceo of Montevideo, Uruguay. It is located on the coast, across the Port of Buceo and on the border with the neighbourhood of Pocitos.

facts.fact: Raúl A. Sichero Bouret designed and built it.
facts.quote: It was designed and constructed by the architect Raul A. Sichero Bouret.

facts.fact: Double-height V-shaped supports and its facade stand out.
facts.quote: This building stands out by the form of its supports (in V) of double height and by its facade.

facts.fact: It was declared of "Municipal Interest" in 1995.
facts.quote: It was declared a building of "Municipal Interest" by the Mayor of Montevideo in 1995.

facts.fact: It is the largest garden in Suzhou and a UNESCO World Heritage component.
facts.quote: At 78 mu (亩; 畝) (5.2 ha; 13 acres), it is the largest garden in Suzhou and is considered by some to be the finest garden in all of southern China.

facts.fact: It joined UNESCO's list in 1997 as part of the Classical Gardens of Suzhou.
facts.quote: In 1997, Humble Administrator's Garden was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site as a component of the Classical Gardens of Suzhou.

facts.fact: Wang Xianchen created it in 1513 on the site of the burnt Dahong Temple.
facts.quote: In 1513, Wang Xianchen, an Imperial Envoy and poet of the Ming dynasty, created a garden on the site of the dilapidated Dahong Temple which had been burnt during the Ming conquest.

facts.fact: The name comes from a verse by Pan Yue about a retired official's life.
facts.quote: The garden was named (first evidence around 1517 ) after a verse by the famous scholar official of the Jin dynasty, Pan Yue, in his prose, An Idle Life

facts.fact: It took 16 years to complete, until 1526.
facts.quote: It took 16 years until 1526 to complete.

facts.fact: The painter Wen Zhengming advised on it and made paintings of it in 1533.
facts.quote: Wen Zhengming wrote an essay Notes of Wang's Humble Administrator's Garden, and painted Landscapes of the Humble Administrator's Garden in 1533 including 31 paintings and poems to commemorate the garden.

facts.fact: Earlier gardens occupied the site, including a Tang scholar's residence.
facts.quote: On the garden's site was first built a garden during the Shaoxing period (1131–1162) of the Southern Song dynasty.

facts.fact: It is a hybrid funicular in Innsbruck that opened 1 December 2007, replacing the 1906 line.
facts.quote: The Hungerburgbahn is a hybrid funicular railway in Innsbruck, Austria, connecting the city district of Hungerburg with the city centre. The current line opened on 1 December 2007, replacing a previous alignment that operated from 1906 to 2005.

facts.fact: Zaha Hadid won an open competition to design the stations.
facts.quote: The renowned architect Zaha Hadid, who had already planned the Bergisel ski jump in Innsbruck, won an open competition to design the stations for the line.

facts.fact: It was a public-private partnership of the city, STRABAG and Leitner AG.
facts.quote: The project was financed and implemented as a public private partnership between the city of Innsbruck, STRABAG and Leitner AG.

facts.fact: The incline changes quickly along the route, from flat to steep.
facts.quote: The new Hungerburgbahn is unusual for a funicular in that, although it does not reach the maximum gradient of its former incarnation, it experiences rapidly changing inclination both during the course of the route and at the various stops, transitioning between a relatively flat southern section (with ramps leading in and out of the two tunnels on either side of the river crossing), and a steeply inclined northern section more typical of a funicular.

facts.fact: It crosses the Inn on an S-shaped cable-stayed steel bridge.
facts.quote: The line crosses the Inn on a 242 m-long (794 ft) S-shaped cable-stayed steel bridge with two pylons, follows the north bank of the river in the St. Nikolaus neighbourhood, then descends into the 445 m-long (1,460 ft) Weiherburg tunnel.

facts.fact: The stations are considered city landmarks.
facts.quote: The new Hungerburgbahn is one of the landmarks of the city, with stations designed by Zaha Hadid, and built by Leitner AG.

facts.fact: Eero Saarinen designed the main and display buildings of the Moline headquarters.
facts.quote: Eero Saarinen designed the original two structures, namely the main and display buildings.

facts.fact: The buildings are clad in Cor-Ten weathering steel and glass.
facts.quote: The main building, display building, and Deere West are clad with Cor-Ten weathering steel and glass.

facts.fact: The seven-storey main building sits in a ravine, reached by footbridges on the fourth floor.
facts.quote: The seven-story main building is located in a ravine and is accessed by footbridges on its fourth floor, which lead east to the display building and west to Deere West.

facts.fact: The display building has an auditorium and a sculpture mural by Alexander Girard.
facts.quote: The display building contains an auditorium with two levels, along with a display area with a sculpture mural by Alexander Girard.

facts.fact: Sasaki Associates designed the landscape with two lakes.
facts.quote: The landscape, designed by Sasaki Associates, includes two lakes.

facts.fact: Saarinen died just after construction began; it opened 20 April 1964.
facts.quote: Hewitt hired Saarinen, whose plans were approved in 1958; Saarinen died just after construction started in 1962. The complex opened on April 20, 1964, and included provisions for connections to additional buildings in the south and west.

facts.fact: It received the Twenty-five Year Award.
facts.quote: It has also received numerous awards, including the Twenty-five Year Award for architectural excellence.

facts.fact: Roche-Dinkeloo added Deere West in 1978, with offices around a glass-roofed atrium.
facts.quote: Roche-Dinkeloo was hired in 1975 to design Deere West, which opened in 1978.

facts.fact: Hans Poelzig designed it in Neue Sachlichkeit style, built 1928–29.
facts.quote: The building was erected 1928–29. It was designed by the architect Hans Poelzig in the Neue Sachlichkeit style.

facts.fact: It is one of eight Poelzig blocks, with apartments and shops.
facts.quote: The completed blocks included 170 apartments and 80 shops.

facts.fact: It was the only Poelzig block to survive WWII completely intact.
facts.quote: This was the only block of the Poelzig-designed neighbourhood that survived World War II completely intact.

facts.fact: Rows of windows and a wide roof moulding structure the facade horizontally.
facts.quote: The building is strongly structured horizontally by rows of windows forming stripes and a wide overhanging moulding at the roof plate.

facts.fact: The facade is ochre plaster with light yellow stripes.
facts.quote: The front is ochre-coloured plaster, with stripes painted on plaster in a light yellow shade.

facts.fact: The interior uses economical materials and the emotional impact of colour.
facts.quote: Following Neue Sachlichkeit design principles, the interior design was characterized by economical use of materials and utilisation of the emotional impact of colour and form:

facts.fact: It was restored 1999–2001 and won a monument-protection award in 2002.
facts.quote: In 2002 the restoration was awarded the "German Award for Monument Protection".

facts.fact: It is now a revival cinema with three screens.
facts.quote: The cinema was originally host to a single screen with 1200 seats. This has since been split into three screens, with each now seating 500, 68 and 43 people respectively.
